source.title: TransRetrieval: Scaling Up Transformer-Based Retrieval for Industrial Recommendation
source.authors: Zhi-Fei Zheng; Yun-Fei Liu; Bin Liu; Qi-Ren Zhu; Han-Bing Liu; Zi-Ru Xu; Han Zhu; Jian Xu; Qi Qi; Bo Zheng

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies the general scaling-law idea to Transformer-based recommendation retrieval, a new setting, and reports a compute sweep. It does not test language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The study measures Recall@2000 against per-target FLOPs, not held-out language-model loss. Its recall scaling results are recorded under fits_no_version. The aggregation, compression, multi-domain ablations and online A/B results do not directly measure the scaling behavior named in the claim and are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the scaling-law idea as motivation and reports that its own retrieval model's Recall@2000 rises log-linearly with per-target FLOPs. It never measures held-out pretraining loss, parameter, token or compute power laws, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. Recall@2000 against per-candidate inference FLOPs is a different construct from the power-law loss form V5 names. The span is about one order of magnitude (0.13–1.91 MFLOPs) with three tabulated points per dataset. The record's 'tests/T3' conflicts with its own finding that every version is untested, so I reclassify it.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that weighted-average aggregation, target-token compression and position-style domain embeddings 'unlock scaling laws for the retrieval stage'. They cite log-linear Recall@2000 scaling (R²=0.82/0.88), state-of-the-art recall, and a 2.53% platform revenue lift in a month-long online A/B test.
record.recipe_differences: Uses recommendation retrieval trained with pairwise learning-to-rank and evaluates Recall@2000 against per-target FLOPs, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy against parameters, tokens or training compute. No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation is tested.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported sweep varies embedding dimensions (32D, 64D, 128D) and layer counts (1L, 3L, 5L), but does not isolate their individual effects.

fits_no_version.finding: TransRetrieval Recall@2000 rises with per-target FLOPs: 0.464→0.657 on Industrial and 0.251→0.473 on KuaiRand. The span is 32D1L to 128D5L, about 0.13–1.9 MFLOPs. Authors report log-linear fits with R²=0.82/0.88.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Transformer-based recommendation retrieval, Recall@2000 increases roughly log-linearly with per-candidate scoring FLOPs over about one order of magnitude.

fits_no_version.finding: Baseline architectures in Table 3 scale differently. KuaiFormer is near-flat (0.485→0.495 Industrial). HSTU rises 0.380→0.527 over 0.13–1.72 MFLOPs. RankMixer rises only 0.452→0.531 over 2.10–150.99 MFLOPs. None of these appears as a row.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recall scaling with compute in recommendation retrieval depends strongly on architecture and feature handling; some architectures show near-flat returns.

record.problems: The scaling outcome is Recall@2000 in recommendation retrieval, not held-out language-model loss. Only three TransRetrieval configurations are tabulated per dataset; the tested compute span is 0.14–1.91 MFLOPs per target (Industrial) and 0.13–1.81 MFLOPs per target (KuaiRand), not several orders of magnitude. No parameter/token allocation optimum is tested. Numeric confidence-interval bounds for the scaling fits are not supplied in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows: the remaining ablations and online results concern feature aggregation, token compression, domain modeling, or deployment impact rather than the scaling behavior measured here.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss, and no language model scaled in parameters, tokens or training compute.
No fit on small runs is used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-budget parameter/token allocation is studied.
Depth and width vary together (32D1L, 64D3L, 128D5L); there is no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
Recommendation retrieval is a new regime, but the outcome is Recall@2000 against per-candidate inference FLOPs, not the power-law loss form. The span is about 1 order of magnitude.
No downstream task performance is predicted from LM scale or pretraining loss.
No sensitivity of exponents or fit choices is examined.

missing.what: Scaling results for the baselines (KuaiFormer, HSTU, RankMixer) at several configurations. These bear only on the fits_no_version finding, not on any version.

record.verdict_notes: The study is recommendation retrieval trained with a pairwise LTR loss. Its 'compute' is per-candidate inference FLOPs, not training compute. The R² values come from Figure 2 fits whose number of points is not stated in the text; only three configurations per dataset are tabulated. No version of the LM scaling-law claim is tested, so no verdict labels are given.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or language-model parameter, token, or compute scaling is measured.
No small-run loss fit is used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization or parameter/token allocation trend is tested.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count is reported.
Although the setting is recommendation retrieval, it reports Recall@2000 scaling rather than the same power-law form in loss.
Recall@2000 is the retrieval evaluation metric, but the study does not test downstream-task performance predictability from language-model scale or pretraining loss.
No sensitivity of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation to fitting choices is tested.

relation.reason: Scaling motivates the architecture, but the measured construct is Recall@2000 versus per-target scoring FLOPs, rather than a quantity establishing any listed claim version.

tranche.reason: The study uses scaling laws to motivate retrieval design and reports its method's recall versus inference cost. Its log-linear recall fit does not test the catalog's power-law loss, extrapolation, allocation, or downstream transfer claims.

source_check.notes: All reported row values and endpoint changes match the text. The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased; their log-linear retrieval scaling does not establish the catalog's power-law claims.
